analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run national health service offering free comprehensive medical care to everyone in the United States.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 12 House Democrats and no Republicans, was referred to three committees and then two subcommittees, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace Medicare, Medicaid, private employer health plans, and other federal health programs with a single United States Health Service that provides comprehensive care — doctor visits, hospitals, drugs, dental, mental health, long-term care — free of charge to every person in the country. The Service would employ salaried doctors and nurses, run its own facilities, and be governed by boards partly elected by patients and workers. It would be paid for with new percentage taxes on individual and corporate income, ending the tax break on employer health plans and voiding employer obligations to provide health coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone in the United States — including the more than 40 million Americans the bill's findings say lacked coverage — would receive comprehensive health care at no charge, regardless of income, employment, or health status. Health workers would get salaried, secure jobs, free training schools, and paid health leave. The uninsured, people with pre-existing conditions, low-income families, and rural and inner-city communities the bill targets for new facilities would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: Declares all individuals in the United States eligible for the Service's care and entitles them to specified comprehensive services without charge [S3].

Requires each community board to maintain facilities for primary and community-oriented care, each district a general hospital where appropriate, and each region a specialized medical facility, with explicit planning to redistribute resources to deprived inner-city and rural populations [S2].
Lists detailed patient rights, including free care without discrimination, choice of provider, privacy, grievance and appeal rights, and access to user advocates [S3].
Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so workers earn one hour of paid health leave per 35 hours worked, to use when they or a dependent need health care [S3].

Finances the Service through progressive percentage taxes on individuals and corporations and a government contribution, while ending the tax exclusion for employer health benefits and nullifying employer obligations to provide coverage once the Service takes effect [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income individuals and corporations bear the new health service taxes. Private health insurers lose their market entirely; for-profit hospitals, managed-care companies, and drug makers lose the private delivery and pricing system. Employers lose the health tax break (though their coverage obligation is voided). Workers' compensation programs would stop paying for care available through the Service.

drawbacks.text: The bill funds the Service with additional percentage taxes on both individual and corporate income on top of existing taxes, a large new tax burden whose total size depends on what the National Health Board budgets each year [S2].

On the effective date it repeals Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, CHAMPUS, and many other health laws, and voids employer health obligations — a simultaneous overhaul of nearly every American's coverage with obvious transition risk [S2, S3].

Prohibits health boards from letting their facilities be used for private care and bars Service employees from private practice, so patients could not buy faster or supplementary private care through the system — an all-or-nothing design that critics said would eliminate choice [S2].

Concentrates enormous power in an appointed National Health Board over facilities, staffing, drug purchasing (including authority to manufacture drugs), and evidence-based care criteria nationwide, with the President able to disapprove board members [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — free, comprehensive care for everyone, including the uninsured — is the largest health benefit any bill in this period proposed, and the patient-rights and equity provisions are unusually detailed. The costs are equally real: significantly higher income taxes on individuals and corporations, the abrupt replacement of Medicare, Medicaid, and private plans for hundreds of millions of people at once, and the elimination of any private parallel option. The bill is honest about its costs but assumes an unprecedented administrative transition would work; it offered no phase-in beyond a single effective date. Whether that trade was worth it was never debated on the floor — the bill died in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees when introduced, then sent to two subcommittees, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the bill on October 1, 1999, joined by Rep. Donna Christensen and Rep. Jesse Jackson Jr., with 11 Democratic cosponsors in total [S1, S4].
It was referred to the Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees [S1, S5].
In October 1999 it was referred to the Health subcommittee of Commerce and the Health and Environment subcommittee of Education and the Workforce [S5].
No further action of any kind was taken; the bill never received a hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private health insurance industry, for-profit hospitals and managed-care companies, and the existing employer-based system all continued unchanged — the bill would have eliminated or absorbed all of them, and its death without any committee action preserved the status quo entirely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and for-profit health care

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Josephine Butler United States Health Service Act on October 1, 1999.

for.name: 11 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the primary committee of referral (Chair Thomas Bliley Jr., R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on October 1, 1999 and sent to the Health Subcommittee on October 12 — no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred.

against.name: Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the portions of the bill within their jurisdiction after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled House committees took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The Service would be the sole channel for comprehensive care, repealing the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program and CHAMPUS and ending the tax exclusion that subsidizes private insurance. The industry's core market disappears under the bill.

The bill's findings blame 'unnecessary and excessive profits' and the growth of for-profit managed care for inflated costs, and it bars private care delivery in Service facilities. For-profit operators would be excluded from the system.

A national formulary would set which drugs are covered, boards would handle purchasing and distribution, and the National Health Board could run its own drug manufacturing facilities — ending private pricing power over a large share of drug sales.

Health workers would become salaried Service employees with secure employment, guaranteed placement, free training schools, and workplace safety committees — but they would be barred from private practice in Service facilities and paid set salaries.
Employers lose the tax exclusion on health benefits and face the new health service taxes, but their obligation to provide or pay for employee health coverage is voided on the effective date.
